intro: I build the infrastructure that makes robot learning work: simulation, dataset curation, and the evaluation harness that tells you whether a policy actually got better. Before that I spent three years on a production autonomy stack for an indoor mobile robot, across every layer of it, from the GPIO driver that moves the wheels to the TSDF mapper that decides where they go.
I am looking for robot learning and embodied-AI roles where the model and the robot are the same problem.

projects.title: Physical-AI infrastructure for VLA manipulation
projects.role: Created the simulation and evaluation framework. Sole author of the dataset curation tool. Authored both model analyses and the team's training runbook.
projects.hook: Built the loop that turns raw teleoperation into a trained manipulation policy: curate, fine-tune, then evaluate in simulation or on real arms through the same code path. The hard part was making a slow policy degrade smoothness instead of breaking the control loop.
projects.problem: The models are open source. Almost nothing between "a teleoperator moved the arms" and "a trained policy runs on hardware" is. Raw recordings are not a training set, there was no way to run a candidate policy repeatably against varied scenes, and nobody had read the candidate architectures, π₀.₅ and OpenVLA-OFT, closely enough to say which engineering constraints were real.
projects.approach: Three layers that close into a loop. A desktop curation tool over the LeRobot dataset format that browses every episode across many datasets, trims them against a film-strip, rebalances the task mix, and runs a live quality report before you pay for a build. A backend-agnostic runner where one control path drives either a MuJoCo scene or the real arms, chosen by a config key, with scene randomisation, goal predicates, a geometric safety gate and remote GPU inference. And underneath both, operation-level traces of both candidate architectures, π₀.₅ and OpenVLA-OFT, verified against live instrumented runs rather than read off the papers.
projects.outcome: Preview went from a blocking per-frame decode to about 150 ms, roughly 45 times faster, by handing video to the viewer instead of decoding it in Python. A representative dataset build dropped from around 600 seconds to 27. The live quality report recomputes in about a millisecond, so it guides curation instead of describing the result afterwards. The OpenVLA-OFT forward trace passed 18 of 18 checks against a live run, correcting three values in my own draft along the way.

sections.heading: The gap this fills
sections.body:
A team wants vision-language-action policies running on its own bimanual arms. The weights and the training code are open source, so the interesting problems are not the model ones. They are: how do you turn a pile of teleoperation recordings into a training set that will not quietly poison the run, how do you evaluate a candidate policy in a way that means anything, and how do you get the same policy onto real hardware without a second codebase.

I built all three, and the useful thing is that they inform each other. The curation tool checks for a failure mode I only knew about because I had traced the model's normalisation code.

sections.heading: Making a slow model safe to control with
sections.body:
Policy inference is far slower than a control tick. The obvious structure, infer then act, either stalls the controller or drags it down to the model's rate. Neither is acceptable on an arm.

The runner instead uses four wall-clock-paced threads that exchange latest values and never block on a slower peer. The backend steps physics and renders cameras into an immutable image bundle that is swapped without locking. Inference runs asynchronously and its result is drained on a later tick. A missing action chunk means hold the last setpoint rather than emit a discontinuity.

The result is the design goal: a slow model costs smoothness, not correctness.

sections.heading: The delta command that walked the arm across the table
sections.body:
The Cartesian impedance controller takes a six-dimensional world-frame delta end-effector command. The obvious implementation composes that delta with the current pose on every tick, which silently ratchets the target forward for as long as the command is held, so one commanded step walks the arm across the workspace.

The fix is to compose once, on a fresh action, into an absolute target, and track that stored target on held ticks. It is invisible until the arm is moving and obvious afterwards, which is exactly why it is documented in the class rather than left as a comment.

The operational-space maths behind it runs as a C++ and Eigen extension: task-space inertia with decoupled position and orientation, a nullspace term, damping-ratio-derived gains. The bindings are deliberately zero-copy, with row-major references, because Python hands over C-contiguous slices and a column-major reference would force a silent transposing copy on every control step.

sections.heading: Collision checking a robot that is always touching itself
sections.body:
The safety gate writes a candidate command into a private replica of the workspace and asks whether the arm would touch itself or the scene. Naively this rejects everything, because collision geometry is a coarse over-approximation and an arm registers contacts at rest that the hardware does not have.

So at each episode start the layer measures the arm's actual post-reset contacts and exempts each pair only up to its own measured depth, plus a small margin. A pair that later penetrates deeper is still a violation, and those links stay live rather than being switched off for the run. The exempt set is logged every episode so the exemption never becomes invisible.

sections.heading: Reading the model, then tooling what I found
sections.body:
I traced both candidate architectures, π₀.₅ and OpenVLA-OFT, operation by operation and checked them against live instrumented runs.

OpenVLA-OFT turns out not to decode at all. It runs a single non-autoregressive pass over a fixed-length sequence whose action slots are zeroed, so at the first layer those slots have queries, keys and values all exactly zero and their attention is a uniform average over everything visible. The action slots are pure positional queries and all content arrives through attention. That one observation explains most of the otherwise strange code on the path. I also measured that the action head's two residual blocks move the representation by about 2.6 percent, because the residual branch ends in a ReLU and most of its units are dead.

The part that paid off immediately was duller. Fine-tuning on new episodes while keeping the original dataset's normalisation statistics means any out-of-range value normalises outside the range the model was trained on, and the normalisation code does not clip, so nothing downstream notices. I found it reading the code, then built the guard for it into the curation tool: load a reference statistics file, check the current selection against whichever bound matches how the model was trained, and name that bound in every message, because the same data flags none of a hundred episodes under one bound and all hundred under another.

sections.heading: The error that pointed at the wrong place
sections.body:
Evaluation runs started dying with a CUDA error reporting no kernel image available, about four hundred lines into a script. Not at model load, which is where anyone would look first.

The cause was that the project pins a torch version whose compiled architecture list stops well short of the evaluation box's GPU generation. It surfaces late because moving a model to a device is a pure memory copy. Nothing executes a kernel until the first real operation, so the failure appears at the first compute call rather than at the incompatibility that caused it, and nothing in the repository checks GPU capability at start-up.

I wrote a standalone diagnostic that prints the compiled architecture list against each GPU, tries three trivial kernels, and surveys every environment's build, so the next person spends a minute on it instead of a day.

projects.title: Production autonomy stack for an indoor mobile robot
projects.role: Major contributor across the stack and primary author of its core algorithm modules, the middleware, and the embedded layer.
projects.hook: Three years on one robot, across every layer of it: the sysfs GPIO driver that moves the wheels, the shared-memory bus that carries the odometry, and the TSDF mapper and planners that decide where to go. The mapping backend was replaced mid-life without touching the planners.
projects.problem: An indoor robot has to navigate an environment nobody surveyed in advance, keep a usable map of it across power cycles, avoid things that move, and do all of it on a mobile SoC with no ROS on board and a real power budget. Holding those layers together is a different problem from solving any one of them.
projects.approach: At the bottom, a Yocto distribution for a Qualcomm SoC with cross-compilation and device-tree work, then a hardware abstraction layer over GPIO, PWM, encoders, I2C and UART, with a co-processor firmware and a PID drive system on IMU-fused odometry. In the middle, a ROS-free publish/subscribe and service bus over shared memory, with a process manager and a watchdog. On top, TSDF submaps carrying occupancy and distance in one voxel, a pose-anchored submap collection that consumes optimised poses from the team's SLAM, D* Lite for global planning and a DWA local planner with a behaviour layer over it.
projects.outcome: A deployed robot that maps, plans, explores and persists its map across power cycles. I authored the seven-stage CI pipeline that gates it, including a performance-regression stage: an in-house profiler times instrumented functions to CSV, and the pipeline pulls the baseline from the package registry and plots each change against it. That is why the optimisation work is verifiable rather than asserted.

sections.heading: The span
sections.body:
The claim worth making about this project is not any single algorithm. It is that the same person wrote the driver that moves the wheels and the mapper that decides where they should go, and that those layers were designed to fit each other.

At the board level that meant a Yocto layer for the SoC, Dockerised aarch64 cross-compilation, device-tree patches and A/B image deployment. Above it, a hardware abstraction layer: sysfs GPIO and hardware PWM, quadrature encoders, motor and servo drivers, a small co-processor firmware for PWM, an IMU client. Then a templated PID drive system with anti-windup and differential-drive odometry that fuses IMU yaw with timestamp interpolation.

Between the embedded layer and the autonomy layer sits a publish/subscribe and service bus built on shared memory rather than ROS, with typed channels, interprocess mutexes and condition variables, and custom serialisation. A systemd service and watchdog keep the processes alive in the field.

sections.heading: Replacing the map without breaking the planners
sections.body:
The first mapping design was a moving local volume feeding a two-dimensional global grid. The local map is a ring buffer sized to a power of two so the volume translates with the robot without copying data, which reduces the index arithmetic to bit operations. It worked, but it could not support persistence or loop closure.

The replacement is a life-long backend built essentially from scratch: truncated signed distance function submaps with trilinear interpolation and the ability to fuse and un-fuse a submap, a hybrid voxel that packs the distance value, occupancy state and Euclidean distance field together so one block traversal serves surface reconstruction, occupancy and clearance queries, and a pose-anchored submap collection that consumes optimised poses from the team's SLAM and rebuilds its spatial hash when they arrive. Distance fields come from the Felzenszwalb lower-envelope transform, refactored into a separable one-dimensional pass for speed.

Swapping a mapping backend underneath a working planning stack is the kind of change that usually becomes a rewrite. It did not here, because the mapper sat behind a common interface chosen at compile time. The same trick applies to the communication layer, where identical algorithm code runs against either ROS topics or the shared-memory bus, so the stack develops on a desktop with ROS tooling and deploys on target without ROS.

sections.heading: Why the planner is fast
sections.body:
D* Lite was chosen over A* because the map changes continuously and prior search results should be repaired rather than discarded. A* was implemented first, optimised, measured, and then archived.

But the algorithm is not what makes it fast. The published description tells you what to compute. It does not tell you that the open list needs an augmented key to live in an ordered map, because D* Lite keys are not unique, or that node lookup needs a hand-written bijective two-to-one-dimensional hash to stay constant time on the hot path. Those two structures are the difference between a planner that keeps up with a moving map and one that does not.

Obstacle distance from the distance field folds into edge cost, so paths prefer clearance instead of hugging walls, and a new path only replaces the current one if it differs by more than a threshold, which stops the visible flapping you otherwise get when the map updates.

The local planner samples a velocity window admissible under the robot's acceleration limits, rolls each candidate out and scores it. On top of it sits a behaviour layer: stuck detection with recovery, retreat on contact, heading alignment at start and goal, and obstacle inflation that scales with current speed, so the robot is conservative when it is moving fast and permissive when it is crawling.

sections.heading: Glass
sections.body:
A depth camera cannot see a glass partition, and an indoor robot meets them constantly. The cheapest correct sensor for a transparent wall turns out to be having touched it, so bump-sensor contacts are fused into the map as occupied voxels at the computed collision point and the distance field is recomputed around them.

It is an unglamorous fix and it is the kind of thing that decides whether a robot survives a real building.

sections.heading: Measuring instead of asserting
sections.body:
Performance regressions are invisible unless something is watching for them. I wrote an in-house profiler that times instrumented functions into a CSV, then wired it into CI as a comparison rather than a report: the pipeline downloads the baseline profiler data from the package registry and plots the current change against it as a build artifact.

That is a materially harder thing to build than a test suite, and it is the reason specific optimisations here, the separable distance transform, single-pass raycasting, reduced hash lookups, avoided allocations in the frontier scoring loop, can be stated as results rather than intentions.

projects.title: Running a learned model on a robot's NPU
projects.role: Created the module and wrote nearly all of it: the on-device inference path, the tracker, and the following behaviour.
projects.hook: A person-following capability with the detector running on the robot's Hexagon DSP. Detecting people is the easy half. Knowing that the person in frame now is the same person you were following a second ago is the half that decides whether it works.
projects.problem: Following a person needs a detector fast enough to run continuously on a power-constrained mobile SoC, a way to hold onto the right person across frames when other people walk through, and a motion estimate good enough to keep going when the detector misses.
projects.approach: A person-landmark network runs on the DSP through the vendor's neural network SDK, with the backend and model both loaded dynamically from config so the model can change without a rebuild, and tensors built by deep-copying the graph's own descriptors so shapes and dtypes follow the model instead of being hard-coded. Detections are thresholded and passed through a hand-written non-maximum suppression. Foot landmarks project to a ground position through the depth image, an HSV histogram gives an appearance model, and association scores squared distance plus a weighted appearance term. A templated, allocation-free Kalman filter carries the target through detection gaps.
projects.outcome: Shipped as a real capability, with the follow distance, search pattern, extrapolation window and association weighting all configured rather than compiled in. Because the detector sits behind an interface with a dummy implementation, the tracking and behaviour layers run and are testable with no DSP and no robot present.

sections.heading: Getting a network onto the DSP
sections.body:
The detector runs on the SoC's digital signal processor through the vendor SDK. Both the backend and the model are loaded at runtime as shared objects named in configuration, so swapping a model is a config change rather than a rebuild.

The part that matters for correctness is that nothing about the model is hard-coded. Input and output tensors are constructed by deep-copying the graph's own tensor descriptors and allocating from them, with sizes and data types derived from the graph. The model's expected input resolution is read out of the graph and returned to the caller, so preprocessing follows the model rather than assuming it.

Per-node profiling walks the SDK's profiling event tree, which is how you find out that a layer has quietly fallen back from the DSP to the CPU. Without that you only see the aggregate slowdown and guess.

sections.heading: The filter was tracking the wrong thing
sections.body:
This is the part I would want to be asked about.

The estimator initially tracked the derived goal pose rather than the person. That works until it doesn't. The goal is a function of the target, the robot's own pose and the follow distance, so filtering it mixes the person's motion with the robot's motion and with the geometry. The estimate degrades exactly when the robot is manoeuvring, which is exactly when you need it.

The correction was to track the person and let goal generation become a pure function of a properly estimated target. It is a design error, found and fixed, and the branch history still shows it.

The filter itself is written from scratch, templated on state and measurement dimension so all the matrices are compile-time sized and the estimator never allocates. It exposes both predict-and-correct and predict-only estimation, and the predict-only path is the one that carries the target through a detection gap for a bounded window before the robot gives up and rotates to search.

sections.heading: Not losing the person in a crowd
sections.body:
Nearest-neighbour association swaps targets the moment somebody walks closer to the robot than the person it is following. That is not an edge case, it is a corridor.

So the association cost is squared distance plus a weighted appearance term from an HSV histogram of the detection box, compared by correlation against a stored model of the target, with detections below a similarity threshold rejected outright. The weighting is a tunable parameter rather than a constant because the right trade-off between same-place and same-clothing depends on the environment.

The unglamorous half is depth. Both feet, one foot, neither foot, and physically implausible separations between them all happen constantly. If the two feet are a plausible distance apart their midpoint is the ground position; if not, the foot nearer the last known position is trusted and the other discarded as a bad reading; if only one has finite depth, that one is used. Every branch has to produce something sane or the track dies, and that logic is most of what makes the module work.

sections.heading: Why this is the answer to one specific interview question
sections.body:
"Can you get a learned model running on a robot?" is the question an embodied-AI team actually needs answered, and it is usually answered with a plan.

Here the conversion and deployment path onto the DSP and the runtime that consumes it were built by the same person, and the result shipped. That is the whole point of including this project: it makes the rest of my model work concrete rather than aspirational.

projects.title: Control and simulation of a soft continuum robot
projects.period: Aug 2022 – Jun 2023 · Master's thesis, IIT Bombay
projects.role: Sole author. Model validation and extension, the simulator, the controller, and the hardware I designed, cast and assembled.
projects.hook: A five-segment silicone robot I fabricated, closed-loop controlled from an overhead camera. My controller needed torque and the servos could not deliver it, so I cast a torque sensor from the same silicone as the robot. Then that failed too, and the fix was to change what the controller commands.
projects.problem: Soft robots deform continuously, so their state is effectively infinite-dimensional. The models accurate enough to trust are too slow to sit inside a control loop, and the models fast enough to run in the loop are only valid for slow motion and specific shapes. I wanted one model that was both fast enough to close a loop and accurate enough to be worth closing.
projects.approach: I represented the planar body as a mass-spring network whose stiffness matrix is rebuilt from the deformed configuration every step, which is what captures geometric nonlinearity at large deflection without paying finite-element cost. I validated it against analytical solutions, a chained beam-constraint model and FEM, then built a predictive controller on it that forms a numerical Jacobian by running five perturbed copies of the simulator in parallel, each snapshotting state, perturbing one input, predicting forward and rewinding. The robot is five cast silicone segments with rigid printed ends, tendon-driven, tracked by markers through an overhead 4K camera.
projects.outcome: Set-point accuracy of 0.3 mm at the tip, with trajectory tracking typically between 0.6 and 0.8 mm, against a vision system that itself resolves pose to 0.35 mm and slope to 0.005 radians. The model matches FEM to within a few percent on tip deflection across aspect ratios, and its first three natural frequencies sit within about 2 percent. The control loop runs at 2 to 4 Hz, which is a pseudo-static controller's honest limit and the thing I would attack next. Awarded a departmental Research Award.

lead_media.alt: Five-segment tendon-driven soft continuum robot lying on a horizontal white frame, each segment a translucent cast silicone core between rigid printed plates carrying three red tracking markers, with tendon cables running along both sides
lead_media.caption: The assembled robot under the overhead camera. The red markers on each segment plate are what the vision system fits position and slope to.

sections.heading: A model that is both fast and honest
sections.body:
The planar body is a square mesh. Every vertex is a node carrying a share of the mass, every edge and diagonal is a spring, and springs act in parallel where squares share an edge. The dynamics are the usual mass, damping and stiffness form with Rayleigh damping.

The load-bearing detail is that the stiffness matrix is rebuilt from the deformed configuration at every step. That is what lets a lumped mass-spring network capture geometric nonlinearity at large deflection, and it is the whole reason this competes with finite elements for accuracy while staying cheap enough to run repeatedly.

I did not invent the mass-spring topology. It comes from my supervisor's earlier work; my contribution was validating it in the large-deformation range and building the first control stack on it. I benchmarked it four independent ways: against linear analytical solutions in tension and compression, against a chained beam-constraint model under end force and pure moment, against FEM for distributed bending across three aspect ratios, and against FEM for the first three natural frequencies.

One benchmark disagrees. The step-response settling value in one axis does not match FEM, by about a millimetre. I reported it rather than dropping the plot.

sections.heading: A Jacobian from seven simulators
sections.body:
The controller is a deliberately simplified predictive controller, and the thesis says so plainly rather than calling it MPC and hoping. At each step it needs the sensitivity of tip position to each of five section torques.

Rather than linearise a nonlinear network with thousands of degrees of freedom analytically, I got the Jacobian by brute parallelism. Seven simulator processes run at once: one plant, one unperturbed predictor, and five step-response predictors. Each predictor advances with the plant, snapshots the full state, applies a perturbation to exactly one input, predicts a second ahead on a coarser timestep, publishes the resulting tip pose, and then rewinds to the snapshot. A compiler node assembles the five differences into the matrix and divides by the step height. All of it inside one control period.

The control increment is then the minimum-norm solution through a pseudo-inverse, saturated on its largest entry with the rest scaled by the same ratio, so the commanded direction is preserved rather than rotated by per-entry clipping.

That pattern, snapshot, perturb, roll out, rewind, is the same shape as a batched rollout worker in a model-based learning setup, which is most of why this project still feels relevant to what I want to do next.

One methodological choice worth stating: the controller's predictor runs a coarser mesh than the plant it controls. The controller is therefore always somewhat wrong about the plant by construction, so the simulation result means something instead of validating itself.

sections.heading: The sensor I built and had to abandon
sections.body:
The controller is formulated in torque. The servos' gear ratio meant torque could not be commanded reliably, only position. So I built the missing sensor: a torsional torque sensor cast from the same silicone as the segments, in a two-part printed mould I designed, with rigid load-transfer ends. I swept its length and diameter against maximum shear stress to trade range against resolution, built several, and characterised each by hanging known weights while an encoder read deflection, getting a clean linear fit over about plus or minus 120 degrees.

Then it failed three ways at once. The range of torque it could transfer was too small to be useful. Optimising the geometry to widen that range sacrificed the resolution the robot needed, and there was no geometry that satisfied both. And because the sensing element was silicone, its properties drifted over time and its fatigue life was poor. I had built a drift-prone sensor to measure a drift-prone plant.

The fix was not a better sensor. While characterising it I had noticed that slope and torque are close to linearly related over the working range. So I changed what the controller commands: the high-level controller still reasons in torque, but its output passes through a torque-to-slope conversion, a low-level slope loop drives the servo position, and the measured slope is pushed back through a slope-to-torque conversion so the predictive model upstream still sees the quantity it needs to simulate forward.

Two conversions bracketing a new inner loop, and the controller never learns that its actuator changed.

media.alt: Block diagram: MPC controller outputs desired torque deltas through a torque-to-slope block into a slope controller, which commands servo positions to the continuum robot; measured slopes return through a slope-to-torque block, alongside six parallel step-response prediction nodes feeding a step-response compiler
media.caption: The re-cut architecture. The two triangular conversion blocks are the whole pivot: the predictive controller still speaks torque while the hardware is commanded in slope. The six boxes below are the parallel prediction processes that build the step matrix.

sections.heading: The material would not hold still
sections.body:
This one is not in the thesis. It is in the commit log, which is arguably where the honest version of a project lives.

Over roughly ten days in April I went from "the Young's modulus should be near 1.8 MPa" to "found the correct value to be around 1.62 MPa" to a commit that reads, in capitals partway through, that there was a significant change in material property between two identical experiments run twelve days apart, and that it needed investigating. The model in the final thesis uses about 1.54 MPa, while every clean beam benchmark earlier in the document uses 1 MPa.

Cast silicone kept curing and its stiffness drifted under me while I was trying to identify it. I ended up characterising hysteresis deliberately, with slowed motion and dwell time at the extremes, to separate that from the drift.

It cost the better part of two weeks and it is the single most useful thing I learned on the project: a parameter you identified last fortnight is not a constant, and a sim-to-real gap is often a calibration that expired rather than a modelling error.

sections.heading: What the numbers are, precisely
sections.body:
Tip set-point control lands at 0.3 mm. Trajectory tracking averages under a millimetre when slow, with the four measured runs coming in at 0.8, 2.2, 0.6 and 0.6 mm; accuracy degrades with speed and is worst at sharp direction changes, recovering to within 0.3 mm once past the corner.

Those numbers sit against a vision system that resolves pose to 0.35 mm and slope to 0.005 radians, which is the floor for all of it. The low-level slope loop is accurate to that 0.005 radian limit.

The loop runs at 2 to 4 Hz with a rise time around a second and a closed-loop bandwidth near 0.25 Hz. That is the honest ceiling of a pseudo-static controller that does not account for the system's dynamics, and it is what I would go after next: there is a half-finished controller in the repository that accumulates impulse-response matrices and distributes a minimum-energy input across the horizon instead, which is the right attack on exactly this limitation.

media.caption: One segment. The translucent core is cast silicone; the tendon running to the plate above it is the only actuation.

projects.title: Robotic charging challenge: reachability-driven arm design
projects.period: Feb 2023 · Inter-IIT Tech Meet 11.0, Silver Medal
projects.role: Nine-person team. I owned the reachability analysis: the collision model, the workspace characterisation, and the link-length iteration driven off it. Teammates owned the inverse kinematics, trajectory time-scaling and the vision pipeline.
projects.hook: A robot arm that plugs a charger into a car nobody parked carefully. I scored every cell of the arm's task space by how many distinct orientations it could reach that cell in, then used that field to choose link lengths. Reaching the port's position is useless if you cannot arrive along the plug's axis.
projects.problem: Jaguar Land Rover's brief was an autonomous charging station: find an electric car's charging port with cameras and plug a connector into it. Two things had to be true at once. The arm's geometry had to reach every plausible port pose, because cars park sloppily and port height varies by model. And the motion had to be self-collision-free and slow enough near a customer's car to be safe. Nine days, nine people.
projects.approach: I described the arm as a parametric table over its link lengths, so changing a link was one edit and everything downstream re-derived. Each link got a collision bounding box measured off the CAD. Then a sweep over the joint space records, for every collision-free configuration, the end-effector pose including its approach axis, producing not a binary reach mask but a count of distinct reachable orientations per task-space cell. With that cheap enough to re-run, changing a link length became a measurement instead of a guess.
projects.outcome: The submission took the Silver Medal. The characterisation gives a usable task space from roughly 0.4 to 0.8 m from the mount, and the orientation-count field is what drove the link-length change. The repository does not record a before-and-after number for that change, so I am not going to quote one.

lead_media.alt: Eight stacked horizontal slices through the arm's task space from 0.5 to 1.2 metres in height, each cell coloured by the number of distinct end-effector orientations reachable there, with a colour bar running from zero to about five thousand orientations sampled at 0.08 radians
lead_media.caption: Workspace characterisation in task space. Each cell is coloured by how many distinct orientations the arm can reach it in, sampled at 0.08 radians. The blue channel through the centre is the region where the arm can get to the point but barely choose how it arrives.

sections.heading: Reachability, not reach
sections.body:
The usual way to answer "can the arm get there" is a binary reachable volume. For a docking problem that is the wrong question. A charging plug has to arrive along the port's axis, so a cell the arm can only enter in one awkward orientation is functionally unreachable even though a reach map marks it green.

So the sweep records the full end-effector pose, position and approach axis, for every collision-free configuration, and the output is a count per task-space cell of how many distinct orientations the arm can achieve there. That field is what you actually design the mechanism against, and it is what made the link-length change a measurement rather than an opinion.

sections.heading: Making the sweep fast enough to iterate with
sections.body:
A four-dimensional joint grid with a full pairwise collision check at every node is expensive, and the first version was exactly that. It was also, briefly, worse than that: an early version had a live plot call and a one-second pause inside the innermost loop, because I was watching it to debug the collision boxes.

The fix that mattered was hoisting the collision check into every level of the nested sweep. If link two's box already collides at a given angle, the entire subtree of joint angles below it is never entered. Same idea as branch and bound. That pruning is what bought the resolution: the final field is sampled at 0.08 radians, which the naive version could not have reached in the time available.

There is also a bug worth owning. In the first version I built the sweep ranges for three joints from the second joint's limits, a copy-paste that silently swept about half the real workspace. It is fixed in the production version. You only catch that class of error by plotting the field and noticing the shape is wrong, which is an argument for plotting things.

sections.heading: What was mine and what was not
sections.body:
This was a nine-person team over nine days, and the repository is upstream-owned by a teammate; mine is a fork.

Mine: the collision model, the workspace characterisation and the link-geometry iteration driven off it, the screw-axis conversions, the workspace plotting, the bridge from the MATLAB planner into ROS, and the Simscape and 3D-world integration.

Not mine: the analytic inverse kinematics with all its branches and singular cases, the recursive Newton-Euler torque computation, the trajectory generation and trapezoidal time-scaling, the per-trajectory energy figures, and the vision pipeline that finds the charge port.

One story from the team's half is worth telling because it is the best engineering moment in the repository and it is not mine. The velocity plan scales a trapezoidal profile in joint space, then checks the resulting link-frame speeds, and if any exceeds the safety limit near the car it shrinks the driving joint's peak velocity and re-plans, looping until the constraint holds. That retry loop is an honest confession that joint-space limits do not translate into a safe end-effector speed, which is the sort of thing you only discover by checking.

projects.title: A warehouse fleet that was not allowed to know where it was
projects.role: Repo owner and majority contributor across six months. I built the robot model and Gazebo arena, the overhead-camera localisation, the fleet manager, and the planner modifications. Teammates built the microcontroller firmware, the reactive avoidance layer and the chute queueing.
projects.hook: Flipkart's brief said the robots could not localise themselves: one ceiling camera had to place the whole fleet. That single constraint forced everything, and it was also the thing that never fully worked.
projects.problem: Build a small-scale version of a sortation fleet and improve its throughput. Each robot had to fit in a six-inch square, carry a cube on a tray that flips to drop it, and take all of its position knowledge from an overhead camera. So: centralised multi-agent planning over robots that cannot sense themselves, with real lens distortion and real timing jitter in between.
projects.approach: I built the parametric robot model and the Gazebo arena with an overhead camera, and the marker-based estimator that turns detections into fleet poses in grid coordinates. For planning I took an open-source conflict-based search implementation and made it plan for real differential-drive robots: I added heading to the search state so that turning costs time, and widened the conflict test by a timestep so two robots arriving one tick apart in the same cell count as a conflict. On the mechanical side I designed the chassis and the later three-wheel omni-drive revision, and wrote the inverse transform from body velocities to wheel speeds.
projects.outcome: We reached round two, a physical arena was built and a bot drove on it. The full multi-agent stack worked in simulation. The localisation never fully stabilised: the last commit in the repository is a teammate still fixing the estimator, and the code ends configured for a single robot after scaling down to debug hardware. There is no throughput measurement, which is awkward given throughput was the brief.

projects.title: Convex MPC for a quadruped, and the QP underneath it
projects.period: Jan – Apr 2023 · Course project, four-person team
projects.role: Four-person team. My contribution was the QP side: the constraint formulation and the rank reduction that made it solvable at rate.
projects.hook: A convex model-predictive controller for a quadruped, with a hand-written active-set QP solver rather than a library call. The interesting part was noticing that most of the constraints were redundant and proving which ones.
projects.problem: Convex MPC for legged locomotion reduces to solving a quadratic program every control step, over ground reaction forces subject to friction-cone and contact constraints. Written naively the program carries far more constraints than variables, and an active-set solver spends its time on constraints that can never bind.
projects.approach: I implemented the standard convex MPC formulation for a quadruped over a prediction horizon, then attacked the constraint set directly: a three-stage reduction that takes a system of fifty-odd constraints on twenty-four variables down to roughly twenty-two to twenty-five, including an epsilon-tightened friction cone so the reduced set stays strictly feasible. The QP itself is a hand-written active-set solver, so the reduction translates directly into iterations saved.
projects.outcome: A working closed-loop model in simulation. I am not going to quote a performance number, because no results were ever saved from it: the deck has no results slide and the repository has no stored trace. What the project actually demonstrates is the constraint analysis, and that stands on its own. The discretisation in the committed code also used an element-wise exponential where the matrix exponential is required, which is corrected but means anything measured before that correction would have been measuring the wrong model.
